Nvidia unveils Rubin Ultra AI chip with 2x efficiency

Nvidia on Tuesday unveiled Rubin Ultra, a data-center accelerator that the company says delivers twice the performance per watt of its previous flagship, as demand for artificial intelligence computing continues to surge across the industry.

Chief executive Jensen Huang introduced the chip during a keynote in San Jose, telling an audience of developers and investors that the new design was built from the ground up for training and running the largest AI models.

The company said Rubin Ultra packs 288 gigabytes of high-bandwidth memory and will begin shipping to cloud providers in the first quarter of 2027, with broader availability expected later that year.

"Every data center in the world is being rebuilt for AI, and efficiency is now the most important metric," Huang said on stage, adding that power constraints had become the biggest bottleneck for customers.

Analysts at Morgan Stanley estimated that Nvidia's data-center revenue could reach 180 billion dollars next fiscal year, driven largely by demand from hyperscale cloud companies and national AI projects.

Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Oracle are expected to be among the first customers, according to people familiar with the plans, although none of the companies commented on specific orders.

The announcement comes as rivals AMD and Intel race to close the gap. AMD recently became a trillion-dollar company on the back of its own accelerator sales, while Intel has struggled to win major contracts.

Nvidia also introduced new networking hardware designed to connect thousands of Rubin Ultra chips into a single system, which the company says reduces communication overhead during model training.

Energy use remains a concern for regulators. Texas recently paused new data-center permits pending a grid audit, and California passed laws covering power and water consumption for large facilities.

Huang argued that more efficient chips are the best answer to those concerns, since they allow operators to do more computing within existing power limits instead of building new plants.

Shares of Nvidia rose 3 percent in after-hours trading following the keynote, extending a rally that has made the company one of the most valuable in the world.

The company did not disclose pricing for Rubin Ultra, but industry observers expect each accelerator to cost significantly more than the current generation because of its larger memory capacity.

Developers will be able to access the chips through major cloud platforms, and Nvidia said its software stack would support existing models without code changes, easing migration for customers.
